newsitem.title: USA: Hilton Hotels raises ITT Corp. bid to $70 a share.
newsitem.headline: Hilton Hotels raises ITT Corp. bid to $70 a share.

text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp. Wednesday raised its hostile takeover bid for rival ITT Corp. to $70 a share, boosting the cash and stock deal to about $8.3 billion.

The new bid came one day after Hilton filed legal motions to prevent ITT from splitting into three separate companies in an effort to thwart Hilton's acquisition of ITT, the New York-based owner of Sheraton hotels and Caesars casinos.
Takeover experts said the move heightens pressure on ITT management because Hilton's offer matches the value that ITT's break-up plan put on its own shares.
"This is really aggressive of Hilton," said one arbitrager, who requested anonymity. "They went right to the magic number. They are not going to nickel and dime. They truly want that company."

Hilton launched its attack on ITT back in January at a price of $55 per share in cash and stock for a value of $6.5 billion. Including debt assumption, the original deal would have cost over $10.0 billion.
The new offer, including debt, is valued at about $11.5 billion and would make Beverly Hills-based Hilton the largest hotel and gambling company in the world.

"Having had the opportunity to review ITT's partial tender offer and break-up plan, we believe our revised offer represents a full and attractive price for ITT shareholders and is vastly superior to the plan announced by ITT last month," said Hilton Chief Executive Officer Stephen Bollenbach.

A Hilton spokesman said the $100 million in cost savings Hilton expects to achieve warrants paying the higher price. He defended Hilton's six-month wait before raising its bid, saying Hilton has always been open to a higher price if only it could discuss a merger with ITT management, which ITT has yet to agree to.

"Now we know what they are going to do. We've seen their plan," said Marc Grossman, Hilton senior vice president of corporate affairs. "Given the cost savings and synergies, we believe $70 a share is fair and attractive."
An ITT spokesman said the company would consider the revised offer.
Since the January bid, ITT has defended itself by selling non-core assets, such as its ownership interest in Madison Square Garden Inc., and by mounting solid defenses to Hilton's legal attacks.

In early July, the company announced it would split into three parts -- one would own the hotels and casinos, a second would operate its telephone directories businesses and a third its educational services. Under that proposal, ITT also would make a tender offer for 26 percent of its stock at $70 a share, and would restructure about $2.0 billion in debt.

Grossman said Hilton's offer is superior because ITT shareholders would receive cash and stock for all their shares, not just for 26 percent of the stock. He also said they would receive shares for the telephone business and directories business that they may not want.
"More important, the only way to achieve the cost savings is by putting the two companies together," Grossman said.
Hilton said it does not expect the higher offer price to dilute its earnings in 1998, when a merger would likely be completed, and it believes the deal would add to earnings thereafter.
Shares of ITT were up $2.5625 at $65.50 following the revised bid while Hilton dropped 37.5 cents to $32.375 by midday.
Some financial analysts expressed surprise that Hilton raised the bid to $70 a share. Most had forecast that the deal would dilute Hilton's earnings at a price higher than around $65 a share.
But Jim Murren, analyst at Deutshce Morgan Grenfell, said he believes a merger, at the higher figure, could add as much as 10 cents a share to Hilton's earnings in 1998.

Other analysts said the cost savings could be higher than the $100 million Hilton is predicting. Indeed, when Hilton announced its intention to acquire Bally Entertainment Inc. last year, it at first saw cost savings in the mid-$30 million range, according to Grossman. But he said the two companies have been able to trim as much as $70 million from annual costs through merging administrative duties, operational overhead costs and reservation systems.

The ability of a merged Hilton and Sheraton hotel company to disband one of its reservation systems completely would be a major way for the companies to cut expenses, according to David Wolfe, of Oppenheimer and Co.
